opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think people often read Clark and Chalmers as if the whole argument hangs on the mind being a kind of information-processing system, so that Otto's notebook counts as part of his mind because it stores representations the same way his brain supposedly does. But I don't think that's really the core of it.

The parity principle, as I understand it, is functional in a much looser sense. It says that if some part of the world is playing the same role in guiding behavior that we'd happily call cognitive if it happened inside the head, then we shouldn't deny it cognitive status just because of where it's located. That's an argument against what you might call skin-and-skull chauvinism. It doesn't require you to say what the role *is* in computational terms. You could be an enactivist, or a pragmatist, or someone who thinks talk of "internal representations" is mostly a useful fiction, and the argument still goes through. The notebook and the biological memory are both reliably available, automatically endorsed, and woven into how Otto copes with the world. That's a claim about patterns of activity and dependence, not about symbols being manipulated.

In fact I'd go further and say that if you take representationalism really seriously, you're more likely to end up as an internalist. If cognition is fundamentally about having a model of the world in your head, then the head becomes the privileged place where the real action happens, and everything outside is just input. The extended mind view fits better with a picture where cognition is something an organism *does* in coupling with its environment, where the boundary of the system is set by the dynamics and not by some prior commitment to an inner theater of representations.

So I see extended mind as fairly neutral on the metaphysics, and if anything it pulls against strong representationalism instead of presupposing it.

r001.rationale: The response says Otto’s notebook counts as part of his mind because it plays a cognitive role in guiding behavior and is integrated into how he copes with the world.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think people hear "extended mind" and they immediately picture the classic Clark and Chalmers paper, with Otto and his notebook, and the way that gets glossed in a lot of philosophy of mind courses is: there's some information processing happening, some of it is in the skull and some of it is in the notebook, and the mind just is that whole computational system. And if that's how you read it, then sure, it looks like it's riding on computationalism, or at least on some view where the mind is a representation-manipulating machine that happens to spill out past the skin.

But I don't think that's actually what's doing the work in the argument. The core move is the parity principle, which is a functional claim, not a computational one. It just says: if some process out in the world is playing the same role for you that an internal process would play, and we'd happily call the internal one cognitive, then we shouldn't deny the external one that status just because of where it's located. That's a point about the arbitrariness of the boundary. It doesn't tell you what the role has to be made of. You could be a hardcore enactivist who thinks cognition is fundamentally about sensorimotor coupling and skillful engagement with an environment, and the parity point still goes through. Actually it goes through more naturally, because the enactivist already thinks the organism-environment loop is the right unit of analysis.

And similarly on representation. The extended mind thesis doesn't require that the notebook contains representations in some robust, content-bearing, Fodorian sense. It just requires that the notebook is reliably available, that Otto trusts it, that he consults it as a matter of course, and so on. Those are dispositional and practical conditions. Whether you want to describe the marks on the page as "representations" is a further question that you can answer however your preferred theory of mind tells you to. A Gibsonian can say the notebook affords remembering. A Wittgensteinian can say it's part of a practice. None of that undermines the extension claim.

So my view is that the extended mind thesis is really a thesis about where the boundaries of the cognitive system are, and it's pretty neutral about what the cognitive system is doing inside those boundaries. The fact that Clark himself leans computational and connectionist is a biographical fact about Clark. It's not something the argument needs. And honestly, I think a lot of the resistance to extended mind comes from people who are reading computationalism into it and then recoiling from the idea that their mind is a Turing machine that includes their phone. If you drop that framing and just ask whether the skull is a principled boundary for the system that does your thinking, I think the answer is pretty clearly no, and you don't need any particular metaphysics of computation to get there.

r001.rationale: The response says an external process such as Otto’s notebook can count as cognitive when it plays the role of an internal process, and describes the thesis as about the boundaries of the cognitive system. This communicates that cognition-supporting tools can be part of the mind.

astra-6.text:
I think those are separate claims. The extended mind thesis is a claim about where cognition happens, or what counts as part of a cognitive process. Computationalism and representationalism are claims about the nature of that process. So saying that cognition can extend beyond the brain doesn’t, by itself, commit you to saying that cognition is computation or that it necessarily involves representations.

You could have a dynamical or embodied account of cognition, for example, where the relevant process involves ongoing interaction between the brain, body, and environment. If some environmental component is sufficiently integrated into that process, you might count it as part of the cognitive system without describing it as manipulating representations.

Now, you still need an argument for why that component is constitutive of cognition rather than merely something cognition depends on. That’s a real issue for the extended mind thesis. But it’s a different issue from whether computationalism or representationalism is true.

r001.rationale: The response says an integrated environmental component may count as part of the cognitive system, but it does not characterize cognition-enhancing tools as part of the mind.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, I think those are separate claims. The extended mind thesis is primarily a claim about where the boundaries of a cognitive process are. It says that things outside your brain, and even outside your body, can sometimes be constituents of that process, rather than just inputs to it. That doesn’t, by itself, tell you that the process is computational or that it involves representations.

You could think cognition is a dynamical process involving an organism interacting with its environment, for example, and still think that some of the relevant dynamics extend beyond the organism. You wouldn’t have to describe that in terms of manipulating representations.

Now, the familiar example of someone using a notebook as memory does invite a representational interpretation, because the notebook contains writing. But that’s a feature of the example, rather than a necessary commitment of the thesis. You can disagree about what cognition consists in while still asking whether whatever constitutes it has to stop at the skull.

r001.rationale: The response says things outside the brain or body can be constituents of a cognitive process, and gives a notebook used as memory as an example.
